title: 22. Interview: Distributed Tracing · Observability & SRE interview
summary: Interview Q&A for Distributed Tracing — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Distributed Tracing interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between a trace, a span, and a log, and how do they relate?
**Answer:** A span is a single unit of work — one HTTP call, one database query, one cache lookup — with a name, start time, duration, tags, and a parent reference. A trace is the tree of spans that together describe one end-to-end user request, bound by a shared trace ID and encoded parent-child relationships. A log is an event emitted by a span: "at this timestamp, this thing happened, with these fields." The relationship is hierarchical — a trace contains spans, and a span contains logs (called span events in OpenTelemetry). The practical distinction is scope: a log tells you what happened at one point in one process; a span tells you what work one service did for one request; a trace tells you what the whole system did for one request. During an incident, the engineer starts with a trace (to localize the problem to one service), drills into the relevant span, then reads the span's attached logs for the exact error message.

**Visual:**
```
Trace (1 request, 1 trace-id)
  +-- Span A (gateway, 12ms)
      +-- Span B (order, 8ms)
      |   +-- Span C (db query, 3ms)
      |       log/event: "row not found"
      +-- Span D (payment, 4ms)
          log/event: "card declined"
```

### Q2. Explain head-based versus tail-based sampling and when you would use each.
**Answer:** Head-based sampling decides at request admission — the root service generates a random number, compares it to the sampler rate (e.g., 1%), and propagates the decision in the W3C `traceparent` flags field. Every downstream service honors the flag, so a sampled trace is recorded end-to-end and an unsampled one is dropped at every hop. Head sampling is cheap (one random per request, no buffering) and works at any scale, but it samples uniformly — errors and slow requests, which are exactly what engineers want to inspect, are sampled at the same 1% rate as healthy requests and become statistically rare. Tail-based sampling defers the decision until the trace completes: the collector buffers all spans by trace ID, waits for the trace to end, applies a policy (always keep errors, always keep the slowest 1%, sample the rest at 1%), and exports only the kept traces. Tail sampling captures 100% of errors and slow requests at the cost of buffering each trace in memory until completion. The state of the art is hybrid: head sample at 1–5% for aggregates, plus tail sampling to retain every error and slow request.

**Visual:**
```
Head-based (decision at root):
  root: random < 1%? sampled=true : sampled=false
  -> propagates flag; 1% of EVERYTHING recorded (incl errors)
  -> cheap, scalable, but errors underrepresented

Tail-based (decision at collector):
  collector buffers trace -> waits for end -> policy:
    if error:           keep
    if latency > p99:   keep
    else:               1% sample
  -> 100% of errors kept, but buffers trace in memory
```

### Q3. What is the W3C Trace Context standard and why does it matter?
**Answer:** The W3C Trace Context standard defines two HTTP headers — `traceparent` and `tracestate` — that carry trace context across service boundaries in a vendor-neutral format. The `traceparent` header has four hyphen-separated fields: version, trace-id (32 hex chars), parent-id (16 hex chars), and trace-flags (2 hex chars, where bit 0 is the sampled flag). The `tracestate` header carries vendor-specific extensions in a comma-separated list, so multiple tracers (Jaeger, Datadog, X-Ray) coexist without stomping each other's data. Before W3C Trace Context, every tracer had its own headers — B3 for Zipkin, `uber-trace-id` for Jaeger, `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` for X-Ray — and a service instrumented with one tracer could not propagate context through a service instrumented with another, breaking the trace tree at vendor boundaries. The W3C standard, ratified in 2020, made context propagation universal: an OpenTelemetry-instrumented service can call a Datadog-instrumented service, and the trace tree is preserved because both sides parse the same `traceparent` header. The practical impact is that mixed-vendor microservice architectures now have end-to-end tracing by default.

**Visual:**
```
traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01
             ^   ^                              ^              ^
             ver trace-id (32 hex)              parent-id      flags
                                                (16 hex)       (01=sampled)

tracestate: vendor1=value1,vendor2=value2

Pre-W3C:   B3 (Zipkin), uber-trace-id (Jaeger), X-Amzn-Trace-Id (X-Ray)
           -> traces broke at vendor boundaries
Post-W3C:  universal; OpenTelemetry <-> Datadog <-> Jaeger all interop
```

### Q4. How does critical-path analysis work, and why is it the most valuable feature of distributed tracing?
**Answer:** The critical path is the chain of spans whose durations sum to the end-to-end latency — the spans on the path from root to the deepest leaf that consumed the most wall-clock time. Computing it requires walking the span tree, identifying for each parent which child contributed the most to the parent's duration (parallel children contribute only their max; sequential children contribute their sum), and recording the resulting chain. The critical path is what makes tracing actionable: "the request took 800ms because the database query on the order service took 600ms, of which 580ms was a row lock wait" is a specific, actionable diagnosis; "checkout is slow" is not. Without critical-path analysis, the engineer sees a tree of fifty spans and has to manually identify which one matters; with it, the tracer highlights the one span to investigate. Modern tracers (Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb) compute the critical path automatically and render it as a highlighted path through the trace waterfall. The reason tracing outperforms logs for latency diagnosis is precisely that the trace tree enables critical-path analysis, which logs alone cannot.

**Visual:**
```
Trace tree (request took 12ms):
+-- Gateway (12ms)
    +-- Order.create (8ms)         <- sequential, on critical path
    |   +-- DB.query (3ms)         <- parallel sibling, NOT on path
    |   +-- Payment.charge (4ms)   <- sequential within Order, on path
    |       +-- DB.insert (3ms)    <- on path
    +-- Kafka.publish (1ms)        <- parallel to Order, max(8,1)=8

Critical path: Gateway -> Order -> Payment -> DB.insert = ~12ms
Optimize DB.insert (3ms row lock) -> end-to-end drops to 9ms
```

### Q5. What is context propagation, and what breaks when it is missing?
**Answer:** Context propagation is the mechanism by which the trace ID, parent span ID, and sampling flag are carried from one service to the next across a process boundary. The sending service injects the context into outbound request headers (the W3C `traceparent` header for HTTP, equivalent metadata for gRPC, message headers for Kafka); the receiving service extracts the context, creates a child span whose parent is the extracted span ID, and continues the trace. When context propagation is missing — because a service was not instrumented, because the calling library stripped unknown headers, because the call crossed an asynchronous boundary (Kafka, SQS) without header propagation, or because a third-party service does not honor `traceparent` — the trace tree breaks. The downstream service starts a new trace with a new trace ID, and the engineer sees two disconnected traces where there should be one. This is the single most common cause of "tracing does not work" complaints. The fix is universal instrumentation; OpenTelemetry's auto-instrumentation packages for HTTP, gRPC, Kafka, and database drivers do this for common libraries automatically. Asynchronous boundaries require explicit instrumentation because publisher and consumer are separate processes connected only by the message body.

**Visual:**
```
Good (context propagated):
  A --[traceparent: 00-abc-def-01]--> B --[traceparent: 00-abc-bbb-01]--> C
  -> single trace tree, 3 spans, 1 trace-id

Bad (context dropped at B):
  A --[traceparent: 00-abc-def-01]--> B (no instrumentation) --> C
  -> A's trace has 1 span; B+C form a separate trace with new trace-id
  -> engineer sees 2 disconnected traces, cannot localize latency

Async boundary (Kafka): publisher must put traceparent in message headers,
  consumer must extract from headers, else trace breaks at queue.
```

### Q6. What is OpenTelemetry, and how does it relate to OpenTracing, OpenCensus, Jaeger, and Zipkin?
**Answer:** OpenTelemetry is the CNCF's vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs, formed in 2019 by merging OpenTracing (a tracing-only API) and OpenCensus (Google's tracing-and-metrics API+SDK). Before the merger, library authors chose between two competing APIs and the choice locked them into one ecosystem; after the merger, OpenTelemetry provides a single API and SDK that every vendor (Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic) exports to. OpenTelemetry is a specification, language SDKs, and the Collector — a vendor-neutral pipeline that receives spans, processes them (tail sampling, redaction, enrichment), and exports to any backend. Jaeger and Zipkin are backends that store traces and render the UI; both accept OpenTelemetry exports. The relationship: OpenTelemetry is the instrumentation layer (generate spans, propagate context, ship to collector); Jaeger/Zipkin/Tempo are the storage and UI layer. A modern deployment instruments with OpenTelemetry SDKs, ships to the Collector, and exports to Jaeger or a SaaS backend. The benefit is portability: switching backends no longer requires re-instrumenting every service.

**Visual:**
```
Pre-2019:   OpenTracing (API)  vs  OpenCensus (API+SDK from Google)
            library authors had to choose -> ecosystem split

2019+:      OpenTelemetry = merge -> single API + SDK + Collector
            |
            v
            OpenTelemetry Collector
            |       |        |        |
            v       v        v        v
          Jaeger   Zipkin   Tempo   Datadog/Honeycomb/...
          (storage+UI backends)

Library authors instrument ONCE with OpenTelemetry -> export anywhere.
```

### Q7. How would you secure sensitive data in traces (PII, secrets, credentials)?
**Answer:** Trace spans can contain anything the instrumented code puts into tags or events, and PII (user IDs, email addresses, payment card numbers) and secrets (API keys, bearer tokens, passwords) frequently end up there because engineers tag spans with request fields for debugging convenience. The risk is that the trace backend becomes a trove of sensitive data accessible to every engineer with UI access, violating GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI obligations. The defense is layered. First, never tag spans with raw PII or secrets — tag with hashes or opaque identifiers instead (e.g., `user_id_hash` rather than `user_email`). Second, use OpenTelemetry's `Baggage` API for cross-cutting context that should be propagated but not recorded as a span tag. Third, configure the OpenTelemetry Collector's `redaction` processor to strip or hash fields matching known patterns (credit card regexes, email regexes, header names like `Authorization`) before export. Fourth, apply RBAC at the trace backend so that only the on-call rotation can view traces containing certain service or tag combinations. Fifth, run a periodic audit script that scans the trace store for high-entropy strings and flags new ones for review. The discipline is to treat the trace store as production data with the same access controls and PII obligations as the application database, not as a debugging scratchpad.

**Visual:**
```
Bad: span.set_tag("user.email", "alice@x.com")
     span.set_tag("auth.token", "Bearer abc123...")
     -> PII and secrets land in trace backend, leak to all engineers

Good: span.set_tag("user.id_hash", sha256(email)[:16])
      Collector redaction processor:
        - strip headers: Authorization, Cookie
        - regex: credit card -> [REDACTED]
        - regex: email -> hash

RBAC: traces with tag service=billing -> only billing on-call can view
Audit: weekly scan for high-entropy strings in span tags -> review
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You deploy a 50-service microservices system and find that p99 latency for checkout is 3 seconds, but no individual service's p99 latency exceeds 200ms. How do you use tracing to find the cause?
**Answer:** The discrepancy between per-service p99 (200ms) and end-to-end p99 (3s) is the canonical case where tracing is indispensable. Per-service metrics show each service's own work but not the cumulative effect of sequential calls through the call graph — fifty services at 60ms each, called sequentially, produce 3 seconds of end-to-end latency even though each individual service is fast. Step one: query the trace UI for checkout traces with latency > 2 seconds, sorted by duration. Step two: for each slow trace, render the span tree and identify the critical path — the chain of sequential spans whose durations sum to end-to-end latency. Step three: examine the critical path for unnecessary sequentiality — is the order service calling inventory, then pricing, then tax, when those calls could be parallelized? Step four: look for "fan-out then wait" patterns where the gateway calls multiple services in parallel but waits for all to complete, when hedged requests or partial results could cut the wait. Step five: look for hidden sequential calls inside services (a loop of N synchronous database queries instead of one batched query). The fix is almost always to parallelize independent calls or batch dependent ones.

**Visual:**
```
Per-service metrics: every service p99 < 200ms  -> looks healthy
End-to-end p99:      3s                          -> user is suffering

Trace shows: sequential chain of 15 calls, each 200ms
  Gateway -> Auth -> User -> Cart -> Inventory -> Pricing -> Tax -> ...
  15 * 200ms = 3s

Fix: parallelize independent calls (Inventory || Pricing || Tax)
     batch dependent calls (one DB query instead of 10)
     hedge requests for slow dependencies
```

### Q2. Your team adopted tracing but the trace UI shows only the root span — no child spans appear, even though the request clearly crossed multiple services. How do you debug this?
**Answer:** A root-only trace means context propagation is broken between the gateway and the first downstream service. Step one: confirm the gateway is injecting `traceparent` into the outbound request — check the tracer configuration and the outbound HTTP client's interceptor; many tracers require explicit registration of HTTP client instrumentation. Step two: confirm the downstream service is extracting `traceparent` — check that its tracer is configured with the W3C propagator (not B3 or a vendor-specific one) and that the inbound HTTP middleware is registered before the application handler. Step three: confirm both services honor W3C `traceparent` — a gateway emitting `traceparent` and a downstream service reading `uber-trace-id` will not connect. Step four: check the sampling decision — if the gateway sampled (flags=01) but the downstream service's own sampler drops, the span is generated but not exported. Step five: check the collector pipeline — a different collector endpoint or tenant means spans may be stored but not associated with the gateway's trace in the UI. Step six: check for header-stripping intermediaries — load balancers, API gateways, or service meshes may strip unknown headers. The diagnostic is to capture the actual HTTP request at the downstream service and verify the `traceparent` header is present and well-formed.

**Visual:**
```
Debug root-only trace:
  1. Gateway inject traceparent?  -> check HTTP client interceptor
  2. Downstream extract?          -> check inbound middleware registered
  3. Same propagator?             -> both must use W3C, not B3
  4. Sampling aligned?            -> gateway flags=01, downstream must honor
  5. Collector pipeline?          -> same endpoint/tenant/storage?
  6. Header-stripping LB?         -> capture packet, verify header present

Fix: register OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation for HTTP client + server
     in EVERY service; this handles 1-3 automatically for common libraries.
```

### Q3. Your trace backend is ingesting 5 TB of spans per day and storage costs are exploding. How do you reduce volume without losing the traces engineers need?
**Answer:** The fix is a sampling strategy that retains valuable traces (errors, slow requests, anomalies) while discarding redundant ones (healthy, fast, repetitive). Step one: measure the current sampling mix — what fraction are errors, slow (top 1% by latency), and healthy. If 99% of stored traces are healthy and fast, the team is over-retaining. Step two: deploy the OpenTelemetry Collector's `tail_sampling` processor, which buffers each trace until completion and applies policy. Step three: define a policy that always keeps errors (status=ERROR), always keeps the slowest 1% by latency, always keeps high-value endpoints (checkout, login, payment), and samples the rest at 0.1%. Step four: deploy head-based sampling at 5% in the root service for capacity-planning aggregates (enough volume for p50/p90/p99 analysis without flooding storage). Step five: set retention — keep all sampled traces for 7 days (incident window), downsample to 0.01% for 90 days (trend analysis), then delete. Step six: review span cardinality — high-cardinality tags (user ID, request ID) explode storage because the backend indexes them; drop or hash them at the collector. The combination typically reduces storage by 90% while preserving 100% of error and slow traces.

**Visual:**
```
5 TB/day -> 90% reduction -> 500 GB/day

Tail sampling policy (at collector):
  keep if status=ERROR                    -> 100% of errors
  keep if latency > p99                   -> 100% of slow
  keep if endpoint in [checkout,payment]  -> high-value
  else sample 0.1%                        -> baseline

Head sampling at root: 5% for aggregates (p50/p90/p99 trends)

Retention:
  0-7d:    all kept traces (incident window)
  7-90d:   downsample to 0.01% (trend analysis)
  >90d:    delete

Drop high-cardinality tags (user_id, request_id) at collector.
```

### Q4. A user reports that their specific checkout request failed, but you do not have a trace ID. How do you find the trace?
**Answer:** Without a trace ID, the engineer must use secondary identifiers to locate the trace. Step one: ask the user (or extract from application logs) for correlated information — approximate timestamp (within a minute), user ID, order ID, error message. Step two: query the trace backend by tag — modern backends (Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb) support `service=checkout AND user_id=alice AND duration>5s AND start_time BETWEEN ...`. Step three: if the user ID is not tagged on spans (it should be), fall back to correlation via logs — search application logs for the user ID within the time window, extract the trace ID from the log line (every log line should include the trace ID for exactly this reason), and query the backend by that ID. Step four: if logs also lack the trace ID, use the request ID (often returned to the user as `X-Request-ID`) to find the gateway log entry, which should contain the trace ID. Step five: if none of these work, the tracing instrumentation is incomplete — every span should tag the user ID, and every log line should include the trace ID. The incident becomes a forcing function to add those tags so the next incident is debuggable in minutes.

**Visual:**
```
No trace ID? -> query by tag:
  service=checkout AND user_id=alice AND duration>5s AND ts BETWEEN ...

No user_id tag on spans? -> find via logs:
  grep "alice" application.log -> log line has trace_id
  (because every log line should include trace_id)

No trace_id in logs? -> find via request_id:
  user's error response has X-Request-ID: req-abc123
  grep "req-abc123" gateway.log -> trace_id

Then: query trace backend by trace_id -> render tree -> diagnose.

Lesson: tag user_id on spans; put trace_id in every log line.
```

### Q5. You have an asynchronous workflow: a user uploads a file, the gateway publishes a message to Kafka, a worker consumes the message and processes the file, then publishes a completion event that another service consumes. How do you trace this end-to-end?
**Answer:** Asynchronous boundaries (message queues) are the hardest case for tracing because the publisher and consumer are separate processes connected only by the message body, and the W3C `traceparent` must be carried in the message headers rather than HTTP headers. Step one: when the gateway publishes to Kafka, it injects the trace context into the Kafka message headers (Kafka supports custom headers per message) using the same W3C `traceparent` format. The publish operation is itself a producer span, with the parent being the gateway's request-handling span. Step two: when the worker consumes the message, it extracts `traceparent` from the headers, creates a consumer span whose parent is the producer span, and continues the trace. Step three: when the worker publishes the completion event, it again injects `traceparent` into the new message's headers, creating another producer span. Step four: the final consumer extracts and continues. The result is a single trace tree spanning the gateway, the Kafka topic, the worker, the completion topic, and the final consumer — even though hours may elapse between publish and consume. OpenTelemetry's Kafka instrumentation handles this automatically when both producer and consumer are instrumented. The failure mode is when the message is published without context, which breaks the trace at the queue.

**Visual:**
```
Gateway (root span)
  |
  +-- Kafka.publish (producer span, parent=root)
      |   [message headers: traceparent=00-traceid-spanid-01]
      |
      v   (hours later, separate process)
  +-- Kafka.consume (consumer span, parent=producer)
      |
      +-- Worker.process_file (child of consumer)
          |
          +-- Kafka.publish completion (producer span)
              |   [headers: traceparent=00-traceid-spanid-01]
              v
          +-- Kafka.consume completion (consumer span)
              |
              +-- FinalService.handle (child of consumer)

Single trace tree across 2 Kafka topics + 4 services over hours.
```

### Q6. Your tracing system shows that a particular database query span takes 600ms, but the database's own slow-query log shows no query over 100ms in the same window. How do you reconcile this?
**Answer:** The discrepancy between the trace span (600ms) and the database slow-query log (100ms) points to time spent outside the actual query execution — typically connection acquisition, network round-trips, or driver-level retries. Step one: examine the span tags for connection-pool metrics — many database tracers tag `db.connection_acquired_ms` and `db.query_execution_ms` separately; the difference is the wait for a pool connection, invisible to the database's logs. Step two: check for driver-level retries — the application may issue the query, get a connection timeout, retry, and succeed, all within one span; the database sees two 100ms queries, the tracer sees one 600ms span. Step three: check for network latency — if the application and database are in different regions, each query has a network round-trip invisible to the database's query log. Step four: check for connection-pool exhaustion — if the pool is saturated, the span includes the wait for a free connection, which can be hundreds of milliseconds and invisible to the database. Step five: examine span events for retry events — OpenTelemetry database instrumentation emits span events for retries, acquisitions, and timeouts. The reconciliation: the span measures application-perceived latency (wait, retry, network), the slow-query log measures only server-side execution; both are correct, but they measure different things, and the difference is the diagnosis.

**Visual:**
```
Trace span: 600ms total
  |--- wait for pool connection: 400ms  <- invisible to DB log
  |--- network round-trip:        80ms  <- invisible to DB log
  |--- query execution:          100ms  <- matches DB slow-query log
  |--- driver retry on timeout:   20ms  <- invisible to DB log

DB slow-query log: 100ms (correct, but measures only execution)

Reconciliation: span measures app-perceived latency (incl. wait, retry,
network); DB log measures execution only. Difference = the diagnosis.
```

### Q7. You are designing tracing for a multi-tenant SaaS where tenants have very different traffic volumes — one tenant sends 1M requests/day, another sends 100. How do you ensure you can debug the small tenant's issues without drowning in the large tenant's spans?
**Answer:** The problem is that uniform sampling captures the large tenant's traffic proportionally — at 1% sampling, the large tenant generates 10,000 traces/day and the small tenant generates 1, making the small tenant's issues statistically invisible. The fix is tenant-aware sampling that allocates sampling budget per tenant. Step one: tag every span with `tenant_id` at the gateway, so the collector can group spans by tenant. Step two: deploy the OpenTelemetry Collector's `tail_sampling` processor with a stratified policy — for each tenant, always keep errors, always keep the slowest 1% by latency, and sample the rest at a per-tenant rate that gives roughly equal trace volume per tenant (0.1% for the large, 50% for the small). Step three: cap the per-tenant rate to prevent a noisy tenant from overwhelming storage — even at 0.1%, a tenant sending 1B requests/day generates 1M traces, so cap at 10,000/day/tenant. Step four: default the trace UI to a specific tenant when debugging, so engineers are not searching across all tenants' traces. Step five: alert on per-tenant error rates independently — a 5% error rate for the small tenant is invisible in aggregate but is a serious incident for that tenant. The discipline is that multi-tenant tracing requires per-tenant sampling and per-tenant alerting.

**Visual:**
```
Uniform 1% sampling:
  large tenant (1M req/day):   10,000 traces/day   <- dominates
  small tenant (100 req/day):       1 trace/day    <- invisible

Tenant-aware tail sampling (per-tenant policy):
  large tenant:  keep errors + slow 1% + 0.1% sample -> ~200 traces/day
  small tenant:  keep errors + slow 1% + 50% sample  -> ~50 traces/day
  cap:           max 10,000 traces/day/tenant

Tag every span with tenant_id at gateway.
UI default: filter by tenant when debugging.
Alert: per-tenant error rate (5% on small tenant is a real incident).
```
